Title:Data Governance for Generative and Agentic AI : Technology, Law, Economics, and Security
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:This book develops a unified governance framework for systems that retrieve, generate, infer, remember and act on information from large language models and retrieval augmented pipelines to autonomous multi agent systems. Eleven chapters and eight appendices integrate three disciplinary lenses-technology, law and economics-across the full lifecycle: data quality, lineage and provenance; global data protection law and intellectual property; the economics of data governance; digital trust, cybersecurity and zero-trust architecture; ethics and responsible AI; governing generative AI pipelines; governing agentic AI and multi-agent systems; data governance in elections and the public sphere; AI regulation across six jurisdictions; and the design of a governance control plane for 2030. Each chapter is anchored in Indian law and institutions while maintaining a comparative, cross jurisdictional perspective.

report.summary: A new arXiv book proposes a unified governance framework for generative and agentic AI, integrating technology, law, economics, and security across the data lifecycle.
report.background: Generative and agentic AI systems do more than produce text: they retrieve data, infer, remember, call tools, and act through multi-agent pipelines. That expands governance risks around data quality, lineage, provenance, privacy, intellectual property, cybersecurity, accountability, and public trust. Regulation is fragmented across jurisdictions, and traditional model-centric compliance does not cover autonomous agents or retrieval-augmented workflows. The book responds by treating data governance as a full-lifecycle, cross-disciplinary problem. Its eleven chapters and eight appendices combine technology, law, and economics, with each chapter anchored in Indian law and institutions while keeping a comparative, cross-jurisdictional perspective. It also proposes a governance control plane for 2030.
key_points: The book offers a lifecycle governance framework spanning data quality, lineage, provenance, global data protection law, intellectual property, economics, digital trust, cybersecurity, zero-trust architecture, ethics, and responsible AI. It connects generative AI pipelines with agentic and multi-agent systems, arguing that governance must cover retrieval, generation, inference, memory, and action rather than only model training.

Agentic AI receives dedicated treatment because autonomy, tool use, persistent memory, and multi-agent coordination create risks that model-level controls cannot address. The framework calls for provenance tracking, access control, auditability, and zero-trust security across agent workflows, so that systems can be monitored and held accountable when they act on data or external services.

The book is anchored in Indian law and institutions but maintains a comparative perspective across six jurisdictions. This makes it useful for readers navigating India’s data protection regime alongside global rules, and it highlights how local compliance choices interact with cross-border data flows, intellectual property, and AI regulation.

A central proposal is a governance control plane for 2030: an operational layer that turns policies into enforceable controls, monitors data and agent behavior, and supports audit and incident response. The book also examines data governance in elections and the public sphere, where provenance, transparency, and trust are especially consequential.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the book pushes governance from a compliance afterthought toward architecture: provenance, policy-as-code, zero-trust security, and audit trails become design requirements for generative and agentic products. Developers may need to document data lineage, constrain tool access, trace agent actions, and build controls that work across multi-agent pipelines. Regulators and enterprises gain a cross-disciplinary vocabulary for procurement and oversight, with India serving as a comparative testbed. For regular users, the payoff is more accountable and transparent AI, but poorly implemented governance could add friction or entrench incumbents. The broader signal is that agentic AI governance is becoming an engineering and legal discipline, not just a policy debate.
report.tools: For provenance and lineage, watch OpenLineage and Marquez; for metadata governance, DataHub and OpenMetadata; for data quality, Great Expectations; for policy-as-code, Open Policy Agent; for supply-chain security, Sigstore and in-toto; for agent tracing, LangSmith or LangFuse. These map to the book’s lifecycle controls and control-plane idea.
